deep.reconstruction:
Context: on the previous page Riemann works with an elementary Abelian integral of the third kind Π(ε1,ε2) on the surface T. It is a function of the point (s,z) that is logarithmically discontinuous at two points ε1, ε2, behaving like log(z−z1) and −log(z−z2). He also notes that the sum of the derivatives ∂Π/∂z over the sheets lying above the same z integrates to log((z−z1)/(z−z2)) + const. On this page he links integrals of the second kind to integrals of the third kind by integrating over the parameter point.

Left column, formula line:
  ∫_{z2}^{z3} f(ε1) dz1 = Π(ε2,ε3),   with Π behaving like log(z−z3) − log(z−z2).
- f(ε1) is a function of the variable point (s,z) that depends on a parameter point ε1 with coordinate z1.
- The marginal note "da f(ε1) unstetig wird wie 1/(z−z1)" says that f(ε1) has a simple pole at ε1 with principal part 1/(z−z1). This makes it an elementary integrand (or integral) of the second kind, Riemann's t(ε).
- Integrating over the parameter z1 along a path from ε2 to ε3 gives a function whose only singularities are logarithmic, at ε2 and ε3. That is an elementary integral of the third kind Π(ε2,ε3).
- Implicit step (mine): locally ∫_{z2}^{z3} dz1/(z−z1) = [−log(z−z1)]_{z2}^{z3} = log(z−z2) − log(z−z3). The single-valued, regular parts of f integrate to a regular part.
- The isolated expression "−(1)/(z−z3)" written under the formula appears to be the check in the other direction: ∂/∂z3 of log(z−z3) is −1/(z−z3). So differentiating Π(ε2,ε3) with respect to the endpoint z3 gives back a second-kind function with a pole at ε3.

This is the standard passage between second- and third-kind integrals by differentiating or integrating with respect to the parameter (the infinity point). It matches Riemann's treatment of t(ε) and ϖ(ε1,ε2) in 'Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen' (1857), §4.

Left column, prose: "Da wollen wir indess hier nicht verweilen, da die andern ... keiner Erläuterung bedürfen ... erst die Theorie der Functionen ... zur Entwicklung bestimmter Formen dieses Integrals Anlass giebt." This is an expository decision. He will not dwell on explicit forms of these integrals, since only the later function theory motivates developing particular forms of them.

Right column: "Wir können daher diese Eigenschaften der Functionen zugleich [...] Die Systeme gleichzeitiger Änderungen der Grössen, durch welche sich eine [...] Function nicht ändert, sollen Systeme zusammengehöriger Periodicitätsmoduln [...] dieser Function genannt werden. Ihr Logarithmus [...]"
- This defines a 'system of associated periodicity moduli': a simultaneous system of changes of the variables that leaves a (multivariable, θ/Abelian) function unchanged.
- The trailing 'Ihr Logarithmus' presumably begins a discussion of the logarithm of the function (θ-function) and its behaviour under such changes.

The next page (No. 10) continues with the general function with m first-order poles, s = Σβ t + Σα w + const, and with the argument principle. This page is therefore draft material for the 1857 Abelian functions memoir.
errors: Possible sign inconsistency. If f(ε1) has principal part +1/(z−z1), then ∫_{z2}^{z3} dz1/(z−z1) = log(z−z2) − log(z−z3). The page writes log(z−z3) − log(z−z2). The jotted '−1/(z−z3)' (∂/∂z3 of log(z−z3)) suggests the consistent convention is principal part −1/(z−z1), or Π with the opposite sign. This is a sign/normalization slip in a scratch note, not a conceptual error.

Unstated: path dependence. The integral over z1 must follow a path on T, so Π(ε2,ε3) is defined only up to periods. Also, f's normalization (e.g., vanishing a-periods) determines which third-kind integral results. None of this is addressed in these scratch lines.

results.what: An elementary integral of the third kind is obtained by integrating an elementary integral of the second kind (simple pole at a parameter point ε1) with respect to the parameter between ε2 and ε3. The logarithmic singularities log(z−z3) − log(z−z2) arise from integrating 1/(z−z1).
results.modern_name: Relation between differentials/integrals of the second and third kind (differentiation with respect to the pole; parameter integration)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann, Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen (1857); antecedents in Abel, Jacobi, Weierstrass

results.what: Definition: systems of simultaneous changes of the variables under which a (multivariable) function is unchanged are called 'Systeme zusammengehöriger Periodicitätsmoduln'.
results.modern_name: Period lattice / period vectors of an abelian (multiply periodic) function

deep.surprise_reason: Draft material for Riemann's published 1857 Abelian functions memoir: the second-to-third-kind parameter integration and the definition of systems of periodicity moduli both appear there. Nothing goes beyond what is known as his.

checkable.sympy: simplify(integrate(1/(z - z1), (z1, z2, z3)) - (log(z - z2) - log(z - z3)))
checkable.asserts: Integrating the principal part 1/(z−z1) over the parameter z1 from z2 to z3 gives log(z−z2) − log(z−z3), modulo branch choices. This is the opposite sign to what is written on the page.

checkable.sympy: simplify(diff(log(z - z3) - log(z - z2), z3) + 1/(z - z3))
checkable.asserts: The derivative of Riemann's Π-singularity log(z−z3) − log(z−z2) with respect to z3 is −1/(z−z3), the jotted expression (result 0).

checkable.sympy: simplify(integrate(-1/(z - z1), (z1, z2, z3)) - (log(z - z3) - log(z - z2)))
checkable.asserts: With principal part −1/(z−z1), the integral reproduces exactly the page's log(z−z3) − log(z−z2) (result 0 modulo branches).

transcription_corrections: The integrand is f(ε1), not f(z1): 'Π(ε2,ε3)' and 'f(ε1)' use ε (point) arguments, with dz1 as the differential.
The isolated 'z − z3' beneath the formula is better read as a fraction '−1/(z−z3)' (or '− ... /(z−z3)'), the derivative of log(z−z3) with respect to z3.
Marginal note reads approximately 'da f(ε1) unstetig wird wie 1/(z−z1) allgemein', i.e. 'unstetig' (discontinuous), not 'stetig'.

Prose reads approximately 'Da wollen wir indess hier nicht verweilen, da die andern ... keiner Erläuterung bedürfen ... zur Entwicklung bestimmter Formen dieses Integrals erst die Theorie der Functionen Anlass giebt.'
Right column: 'Systeme zusammengehöriger Periodicitätsmoduln ... dieser Function genannt werden'; the final word may be 'Ihr Logarithmus' (uncertain).
